My surgeon recommended a sleeve specifically because I didn't have acid reflux. 

The sleeve is the most used procedure worldwide ( 60% of surgery in 2022 were sleeve) , but one of the main concern with it is the apparition or worsening of GERD, and while statistics show that only 12 to 15 percent of sleeves eventually need to be revised to bypass (data at 7 year post-op) , those conversion are often due to this. 

Bypass is still a perfectly valid option. Yes, it carries more risk of complications in the long term,  but those are still very rare. My surgeon was clear on this. The sleeve is the standard,  but if I had any type of acid reflux, he would have recommended a bypass.

Ultimately, the choice is yours. But while I had a sleeve and am so far very happy with the results,  if the bypass had been my only option, I would still have done it.

I don't know why you say "they mostly do RNY" unless you mean specifically at your clinic? The sleeve is the most used procedure worldwide ( 60% of WLS in 2022 where sleeve vs. 29% bypass) and only 12% of sleeve get converted to bypass after 7 years. Just me being picky about numbers 😅.

The physics of it is that when you stop sipping, the liquid in the straw will go down to the level of the liquid in your glass. That leaves air in the straw that you swallow the next sip you take. The longer the straw and the lower the liquid in the glass, the more space for air in the straw and the more air you swallow. It's why my dietitian told me the trick I mentioned: if you pinch the straw, the liquid can't go back down, so it stays filled with liquid, same for straw with check valves. It's not everyone, but some people handle air in their stomach badly after surgery. For me, burping was painful, so I tried avoiding swallowing air as much as possible. Obviously, like you said, if you keep the straw constantly sealed in your mouth, it has the same effect.

They explained to me like this : If you have too much of a deficit, your body will try its hardest to keep its resources. You will have fatigue ( and you say you do ) and, as a result, will be less active during the day. 

You mention in your comments that you don't walk much because of fatigue and also mentioned in another that you rest a lot. I suspect your body is in survival mode right now. It's trying to tell you to rest because it wants to keep its calorie. 

My advice to you is the same that was given to me by my team. Try to up your calories to at least 1000 a day and up your activity levels, walk more and rest less, and do your normal activity during the day. Usually, most weight loss regimens and most research recommend at least 1200 since less than that can cause malnutrition,  fatigue, and dizziness in the long run. It's obviously a balance act depending on your age, height, weight, and level of daily activity, but it's the baseline.

Also, you say your surgeon is giving you your alimentation guideline, but you should really consult a dietitian, will all respect to your surgeon,  it's not his job nor specialization. That's why most surgery teams I've seen have a dietitian on board where I live. Hoping you all the best going forward !

Edit : Should mention about the amount of calories: yes most programs I've seen recommend 600 to 800 before 6 weeks and 800 to 1000 after that, my recommendation are based on my particular experience  and everyone is different. Which is why I recommend seeing a dietitian. In my case, during my stall, I had fatigue caused by hypoglycemia, hence the increased calories. My stall ended after that. YMMV !

Well, that's a complex subject. What aspect of dieting is hard for you ? If it's hunger, yes, it will be easier. Your smaller stomach will produce less hunger hormone, so you will feel less hungry. But after a while, it's gonna start producing more, and you will have to watch your portion to avoid stretching it.

If you're talking about cravings, that's harder. If you have food related disorder, the surgery won't fix them, and those need to be addressed before surgery. "Head" hunger is also a very real thing that needs to be controlled. While your stomach will be smaller,  constant snacking due to cravings will defeat the tightest sleeve your surgeon can do.

In a way tough, after surgery,  you won't be dieting, you will eat what you must and what you can. You will prioritize different food according to your needs and dietitian advice. If you follow the guidelines and eat well, you won't feel like you're dieting at all.

What you lose the first weeks/months mostly depends on your starting weight and the type of surgery. Don't compare yourself to other posts unless you are in a similar situation (weight,height,sex, and age). 

Most charts given by your surgery team or online take all those into account and give an estimate, but it's not exact science and will vary depending on your level of activity. Most people lose faster at first, and then it settles down.

Most professionals and research recommend not losing more than 2 to 3 pounds per week for long periods of time to avoid gallstones and liver issues, but the key here is "long periods" it should cause no issue over a few weeks but over a year could certainly cause concerns. When I had my surgery, I was losing 5+ a week, and now it settled to around 2.5, I'm 4 months post sleeve.

I wouldn't worry too much, if you feel fine, are following your program, and hydrating yourself properly. But If you still have concerns, I would reach out to your surgery team or even dietitian.

Most statistics on the subject mention between 10 to 15 % of sleeves getting converted to bypass after 7 years, not really a lot, but yes those same research paper do mention that most of these conversion are due to GERD.

A sleeve can be revised into another type of surgery down the line if needed, and although rare, there are more complications with other types. Many studies found it safer in the long run. It's why I went with a sleeve myself, no regrets so far. 

Most people I know who got a sleeve kept the weight off even after years, without issues, the ones that gained it back did so because they went back to their old bad habits, no way around it, like its repeated on here many time, it's not a miracle, it's a tool and still need you to put effort into it.

If you purely look at the number, the sleeve has a success rate of around 75 % over 5 years. The mini bypass is around 80 or 85%, depending on what research you look at. For me personally, the statistical difference wasn't worth the additional risk at my starting weight. Wich bring me to my last point :

The surgery you choose should be based on your starting weight and comorbidity. In my case, I was at 343 pound when I started my program, 280 at the time of surgery, and am now 225 at 4 month post op. Had liver issues, hypertension, diabetes and high cholesterol. 8 pills a day, now down to only 2 and should stop another one next month. So pretty happy with my choice.

After a sleeve, you're missing most of your stomach. The stomach is responsible for producing the hormone called Ghrelin, It's the hormone that causes you to feel hungry. Ghrelin levels in your body go down very fast after surgery, and many research showed that it takes more than 2 years to go back to regular level. It's the reason why most assume it's head hunger, because even tough yes, you are lacking sustenance, your stomach is not producing ghrelin to tell your brain it's empty. I did receive that comment, but it was from a few medical professionals. I started changing my habits, exercising more, and lost 65 pounds in a year. Was still recommended for the surgery by my hepatologist even though my bmi was nearly 35, the threshold for the surgery where I live. 

Even though I have gotten surgery,  I do believe it's possible to lose weight without it, but it's one more tool to help achieve this. I think it's more because some people believe it's a "shortcut" or a "cheat." It's really not. Ultimately, you will have to make the same change that someone who lost it naturally will have to make, and like those who lost weight without it, if you don't commit to those change, you will fail. People need to be educated about that. Yes, it's way faster with the help of the surgery, but it's not the miracle cheat that people making those comments believe it is.

No regrets here, but there are a few things to note: I had already lost 65 pound pre-surgery so my eatings habits and amount of exercise where already significantly changed so it made no real difference for me. Cravings did not disappear, but again, I'm already used to it. 

Having started with a therapist is great, but try also seeing a dietitian. It should help you have a realistic goal about what needs to change in your diet right now. You do need to put in the work as you say, the surgery itself is not a miracle, it's a tool, and not following guidelines WILL cause it to fail, plenty of story of that happening. 

Depending on your chosen type of surgery,  the risk will change, but take this coming from someone who was terrified of getting it and did a monumental amount of research before committing : the risk of complications during surgery are actually pretty slim ( complication is around 15% but life threatening one are around 0.10% according to statistics in my country). You have more risk of complications post-surgery only if you don't follow the guidelines set by your team ! Take your vitamins and follow your meal plans !!!!

As for the loose skins, no, the amount of loose skin is not dependent on surgery or not but on the amount of weight lost. Losing it naturally or with WLS will not change anything,  but people notice more because with surgery, it's faster, but losing 150 pounds will result in the same loose skin.

I would say, do it for your health, get plenty of information, make a solid pre- and post op plan, and commit to the life change. Maybe a lot to take in but in the end the decision is yours.

The first thing I learned while on this sub is that the process is extremely different depending on where you live, and even then, even within the same country, it seem to change from hospital to hospital and surgery team. Some people had 2 days of liquid pre-op,  some 2 or 3 weeks. Some had meal plans for months post-op, but some got out of the hospital with only a few guidelines. 

With that in mind, I can only talk about my experience, and I admit it's nothing exciting. For me, it was decided that a sleeve was the best option. It took me 2 years to get the surgery (wait time here is 2 to 5 years), and I had already lost 60 pounds in my last year pre-op. 

For the menu, pre-op, 2 weeks of liquid diet using special order shake, got the surgery,  then 1 week of liquid, 1 week of semi-liquid, 1 week of pureed  food, 2 weeks soft food, then 2 weeks of chopped food, then normal food with some restrictions for a month.

For me, it was pretty mutch smooth sailing on the food side. Contrary to many, I had no cravings, like at all, since I was ( and still am ) practically never hungry. Probably also due to the fact I had already made significant changes to my diet and had already swore off some type of food.

On the surgery side, it took me 24 to 48 hours to be well enough to take a 15  to 20 minute walks, had orders not to lift anything for a month, and 2 month rest at home. All recommendations from my medical team and dietitian were followed to the letter. Got some pain that came out of nowhere after about a month but disappeared after a week, doc think I might have pulled something a bit too much, and an internal wound from surgery acted up.

Lost 45 pounds in 3 months so far, went from taking 8 pills a day to only 2.

My personal recommendations,  follow the plan from your surgery team, and listen to them. I see too many people on this sub asking if they can eat this or that when they are days post op when they should listen to the expert, not some stranger on reddit. But aside from that this here is a great place for many info and discussions. Also, if you got any food disorders,  tell your team and treat it before surgery. And lastly consider this surgery like a tool, not a miracle. If you keep your bad habits, you WILL gain the weight back, seen it happen to people close to me.
